It has been revealed that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

It has been revealed that let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Industry observers note that place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too swiftly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

Industry News: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop.
  • According to recent reports, newly introduced in this upgrade: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options.
  • A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop. But the best cutting boards do more than just protect your counters during food prep—they provide a stable surface when you’re vigorously chopping and act as a protective surface that prevents prematurely dulling the blades of your kitchen knives. Cutting boards come in a variety of materials: plastic, wood, rubber, even glass and metal for inexplicable reasons. After testing dozens of boards of all sorts of materials over the course of six years, we have found five favorites. Read on to find out which might be best for you as well as how we tested and what we look for in the cutting boards we want to use every day.

According to recent reports, newly introduced in this upgrade: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options. They’re easier on knives and more beautiful to keep on the counter. And our new top pick is reasonably priced as end-grain boards go. For more on what makes end- and edge-grain boards different, click here. And if you’re looking for a quality (but truly inexpensive) wood board, we’d encourage you to look at these two Boos boards. They’re edge-grain, so they’ll wear your knives more promptly, but Boos makes almost universally great cutting boards.

Maple End-Grain Cutting Board (18" x 12").

A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment. A good wood cutting board can last decades and decades, and since it will likely live permanently on your counter, function as a key aesthetic component of your kitchen. Our editors have used this heavy-duty piece for over a year in their home kitchens, and even after daily use, it shows little to no wear and only minimal staining.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: The craftsmanship on the board is apparent as soon as you take it out of the box. The offset pattern of the individual pieces of wood is striking (as it is on most end-grain boards). And its construction feels smooth and solid.

Recent findings suggest that as an end-grain board, it’s easy on knife blades, leaving them sharper than a less expensive edge-grain board. The real highlights, beyond the pure aesthetics, are in the small design features, though. Senior shopping editor Noah Kaufman has been using it in his home kitchen since June of 2025 and has found it the most stable board he’s ever used. That’s thanks to the addition of four grippy silicone-tipped feet on one side (you can order a Boardsmith without the feet, but you’d be giving away that stability). Those feet also raise the board up a little higher on the counter—which prevents the underside from retaining moisture and warping—and for Noah, they elevate the board to a very comfortable cutting height. It’s also reversible, with an effective, though not too deep, juice groove on the side of the footed side.

In a recent development, boardsmith’s end-grain boards are very customizable. They come in four sizes (we tested the 18" x 12" x 2", but the largest—24" x 18" x 2"—would make a beautiful always-out piece), three wood types (in addition to the maple, we tried walnut and cherry), and you can opt for features like juice and finger grooves. The feet are also optional, though they’re included by default, so you have to check a box if you want a board without feet.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Again, this board is heavy, which makes it sturdy, but also a bit of a chore to clean. Because it’s wood, it also requires some upkeep in the form of oiling and buttering (the brand’s Board Butter has kept the surface of the Noah’s board in tip-top shape through months of use). Finally, while the feet are a vital feature, they do make the board a little less attractive if left on the counter with the juice groove facing up. But using the groove is a less frequent use than regular slicing and chopping, so you’ll be more likely to leave it feet side down—or at least turn it back over after you’re done cutting and cleaning.

In a recent development, in the long run: With long-term testing of a full year, the Boardsmith has stood up in a way that justifies its high price. It’s held on to minimal stains, and with a bit of oil and wax every three to four weeks, the board looks as beautiful as it did when it arrived.

R-Board Series Rectangular Wooden Maple Cutting Board, 18”x12”.

Boos boards, as they’re commonly called, are pretty much the gold standard for wood cutting boards, and this relatively affordable maple cutting board is a dream to cut on.

What we love: Though maple is a hard wood, the cutting surface is smooth and has the perfect amount of give. In our testing, it seemed to almost embrace the knife blade with each chop. The board didn’t retain any food odors and it was easy to hand-wash (never put a wood board in the dishwasher!). Even beet juice disappeared after a good cleaning.

Boos Blocks come in many different sizes, we’ve found that the 18x12" size is just right for most home kitchens. This board is from the brand’s R-Board series, and it’s substantial without being too substantial. There’s plenty of room to carve a roast chicken, but it’s small enough to slide into the cabinet where you keep your sheet pans (a half-sheet is 18x13") as long as you don’t have too much else in there. At 2.25" it’s the tallest (thickest) cutting board we tested, and it will add significant height to your cooking zone, which is something shorter home cooks should always keep in mind when choosing a chopping board.

Sources indicate that what we’d leave: Though not necessarily a negative, this board is on the heavy side (10 lb.), and it does require frequent oiling to keep it in tip-top shape. Boos recommends their proprietary Mystery Oil and Board Cream, and if you buy directly from the brand, you can bundle the care products with the board.

What we love: Sonder’s board is beautiful, and like the Boardsmith, it features end-grain construction, which is easier on knives because they slide between the wood fibers, avoiding friction with the hard surface. End-grain boards also “self-heal,” which means that the fibers come back together after having been sliced—and I found that after rigorous use in a week of endless chopping tests, this board came out looking as beautiful as it had when it came out of the package. This board is made of American walnut and constructed in the US.

The Sonder board also has some clever design elements: It’s hard to find an end-grain board that features a juice groove at this price point (the Boardsmith below, for example, costs almost $100 more). Flip the board over, and on the other side, it features three carved-out compartments, so you can slide chopped food to the side as you prep, keeping ingredients contained, separated, and out of the way. Those compartments can also be used for a fun charcuterie board setup: Use them to hold sauces and condiments or as a landing place for olive pits. Both sides of the board feature grippy rubber feet, and I found that this board stayed steady and level on the countertop even during heavy-duty chopping.

This board was less cumbersome to take to the sink and hand wash than many of the large end-grain boards we tried. It has ergonomic handles carved into the sides, which makes for easy transport despite its heft and size. And because it’s a dark-colored wood, it demonstrates less sign of staining than other wooden boards.

It has been revealed that what we’d leave: There’s not much fault to find in Sonder’s board beyond the standard caveats that an end-grain cutting board requires maintenance in the form of regular oiling and must be hand-washed. The prep grooves are a nice feature, but they aren’t as useful if you’re used to using a bench scraper, since it can’t fit in them. At $179, the Sonder is a bit pricey, but the benefits of end-grain over a cheaper edge-grain board are worth the bump up. If you’re concerned about price primarily, you should opt for the plastic Oxo board recommended below. Because of the carved-in prep containers on one side of the board, you have limited chopping space (but you always have the option to use the other side, which offers a full surface).

Industry observers note that what we love: Senior reviews editor, Olivia Tarantino, owns three types of cutting boards (wood, composite, and the MK Midi), and the Midi is the one she grabs for anything short of a full dinner. “It’s closer to midsize than small, which makes it more versatile than a mini board that’s only good for smashing garlic. I can dice a whole onion, slice a tomato, and even fit a mise en place of scallion, ginger, and garlic. Because it’s nonporous, it’s my pick over wood for wetter ingredients, since I can toss it in the dishwasher when I’m done,” she notes, noting that she owns the white color and there’s no staining after eight months. The one downside worth noting is that the surface is a bit harder, which can be tougher on knives.

Adding a smaller board like this to a kitchen that already has a large wood cutting board can help for small prep work like slicing fruit, vegetables, or ingredients like garlic without having to clean your significant board in between.

What we’d leave: We wish that Material would add feet to the larger version of the board. If it’s all you’ve got, a small cutting board can be frustratingly limiting. Also, after years of working with Material’s cutting boards in their homes, our editors noted that they will show visible wear and tear in the form of slice marks and small stains. This is inevitable for any plastic (or similar) cutting board.

Good Grips Plastic Utility Cutting Board.

What we love: This plastic cutting board from Oxo is very popular in the BA Test Kitchen. It’s budget-friendly and dishwasher-safe and comes with a juice groove. At 14.75" x 10.4", it’s a good size for meal prep, the plastic cutting surface is nonporous, and silicone strips run the length of both short sides to help keep it in place on the counter when cutting. It’s also reversible with one side offering a channel to catch meat juices.

What we'd leave: The Oxo isn’t very attractive, so you wouldn’t want to use it as a serving board. Also, the longevity of a plastic board like this is only a couple of years, and if you chop too rigorously, the board has been known to shed plastic particles. If you are concerned about plastic use in the kitchen, this isn’t your board.

Yoshihiro Hi-Soft High Performance Professional Grade Cutting Board.

Rubber cutting boards are seen more often in professional kitchens than home ones, but if you’re looking for something large and durable, and you don’t want to have to bust out your knife sharpener regularly, consider this Hi-Soft rubber board by Yoshihiro. It’s very knife-friendly, and cutting on it feels nice. It stays in place on the counter, and unlike another rubber board we tested, it doesn’t have a rubber tire odor.

Sources indicate that what we love: There are a couple of reasons chefs like food-safe rubber cutting surfaces. For starters, because rubber has a little give, the cutting surface flexes ever so slightly to the knife edge versus wearing it down like a hard surface would. Both synthetic and natural rubber are also nonporous, so they’re easier to sanitize than wood boards and are often used by sushi chefs for that reason (conversely, wood cutting boards are actually health-code violations in some cities).

In a recent development, what we'd leave: Though sanitizing the surface is easy, large rubber boards can be harder to wash because, in addition to being substantial, they are also heavier than, say, plastic, and the rubber material must be washed by hand. Rubber cutting boards can also hold on to stains more easily than plastic.

In the long run: With its light color this board has shown a bit of staining and evidence of knife blades running across it. But all things considered, it’s cleaned up very well and proven an excellent companion to an always-out end-grain wood board.

Before getting the knives out, we researched chopping boards and narrowed down a selection that included a wide range of plastic, rubber, and various types of wood boards that ranged from about $10 to almost $300.

To assess the boards’ durability and stability, testers chopped a pound of carrots, diced a large onion, and minced fresh ginger. Testers also cut steamed beets on each board so they could see how much (or how little) each board held on to stains. We chopped lots of garlic on the boards and watched out over the course of the days and weeks of testing for odor retention on the boards. Finally, we washed each board according to the directions and oiled the wood boards that called for it.

Sources indicate that here is an example of the kind of staining you can expect with a wood cutting board. A good scrub with some coarse salt and lemon juice will help take care of this.

These are the qualities we looked for in the best cutting boards.

Industry observers note that we recommend that home kitchens have one large cutting board, ideally around 20" x 15". Additionally, it’s useful to have some supplemental smaller plastic or wood cutting boards (in the 16" x 12" and 12" x 8" ranges) that are easier to transport to the sink for washing or that fit in the dishwasher. You’ll have your bases covered when you have a large board that can take on any large cooking prep task without risk of vegetables flying all over the kitchen, or upon which you can plop a giant piece of meat for carving—but also some small boards that can be used daily for lighter prep, eliminating the need for a daily full-scale clean of your large board.

In a recent development, during testing, I also looked out for board height; if your board is too tall, it adds too much height to the counter, making it awkward for shorter home cooks to get a good angle when cutting. A too big or too heavy board is also hard to clean and move.

We recommend rubber, wood, and plastic cutting boards. There’s a trade-off involved in selecting the right hardness level for a cutting board. A material that’s too hard will have you busting out your knife sharpener more often than you should, while a board that’s too soft will end up with cut marks so deep you may no longer have a smooth surface—and it will be harder to clean and sanitize. So you want a durable surface that will feel nice to cut on and have some give. For wood cutting boards, we prioritized boards made with American materials. That’s particularly crucial because wood sourced abroad is often less sustainably sourced, first because it needs to be shipped overseas, and second because the US has more rigorous forestry regulations than some other countries. For a pro-and-con comparison of the various cutting board materials, scroll farther down the page.

According to recent reports, if the board had a special feature, like grippers or a juice channel, we evaluated how functional the features actually were. We measured the amount of liquid the juice grooves held and used any prep compartments.

Chop-N-Slice Series Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board, 18" x 12".

According to recent reports, if you have your heart set on a Boos Board but don’t have a lot of space or want to spend a lot of money, this reversible board from the John Boos Chop-N-Slice series is a high-quality board with a pretty low price tag. It’s made of durable maple wood and arrives oiled (it only barely held on to stains from steamed beets). It’s only 1.25" thick, which contributes to its low price. Though it’s not too big or heavy, it has handle grooves on both ends, which can be helpful if you’re carrying a loaded board. Right out of the box, we felt the board was a little rough, but with a touch of seasoning, it significantly improved.

Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board.

Recent findings suggest that this end-grain cutting board was a joy to chop on thanks to its soft and responsive surface—it genuinely felt the best of any of the wood boards we tested. Chopping feels ergonomic and your knife feels protected. The board is also beautiful and would stand proudly in a permanent place on anyone’s kitchen counter. When it arrived, it felt dry and chalky, so it immediately needed to be oiled and treated, whereas the winning end-grain boards felt more ready to go out of the box. And unlike the Boardsmith and Sonder boards, it doesn’t have a juice groove.

It also seemed slightly uneven or warped from the beginning: The board wobbled back and forth ever so slightly during rigorous chopping, making a slight clanking noise. This was almost imperceptible, and since we’ve used Boos boards over the years and loved their stability and durability, we think it’s likely the flaw of the particular board we tested. So we’d still absolutely recommend Boos end-grain boards.

Large End Grain Prep Station Acacia Wood Cutting Board.

This inexpensive end-grain board comes highly recommended by other review sites, and at $72 at the time of writing, it’s an excellent value for an acacia wood board. Its dark color makes it resistant to showing stains, and after being put through its chopping paces, it had no scratches. However, the board did arrive with a visible scratched-up patch on its lower right corner. Even though it was an end-grain board, I didn’t find it as soft or responsive as the Boos above or either of our winning boards. And the wood isn’t sourced domestically. Still, this is a solid value option.

If you’re looking for a large and inexpensive board, this 20" x 15" option from TeakHaus is a good choice. The high-quality edge-grain teak looks great, and the darker wood won’t show stains like lighter-colored wood boards do. Cutting felt comfortable, and one side of this reversible board features a juice groove. It’s an inch-and-a-half tall, and that combined with the size makes it pretty bulky. Also, the smell of ginger lingered on this one a bit after we hand-washed it.

Industry observers note that this Kickstarter-funded design isn’t just a cutting board; it’s a whole modular prep station. The cutting board has magnetic sides, onto which snap carved wood prep bowls fitted with stainless-steel containers (or silicone liners, depending on which package you opt for). Those bowls also stack nicely on top of the board for storage, and everything can be arranged and rearranged at the cook’s convenience.

The design here is clever: It’s satisfying to move the board and containers around because everything fits together in a delightful little puzzle, and attaching the prep bowls produces a satisfying click. The magnetic connection is very secure, and it’s helpful and convenient to have little prep bowls available for sweeping away items as you chop them.

You can select various attachable container sizes, and there’s even a large one that runs the whole length of the cutting board that can be used to set up a dredging station for chicken cutlets. You can also buy lids that fit the containers so that they can go right in the fridge to store leftover prepped items, or sauces you made ahead of time for a dinner party.

We like a lot of what’s going on here, but the board’s edge-grain maple construction doesn’t feel high-quality—it was chalky and rough upon arrival. The system is available in a variety of wood types, so maybe the walnut or Brazilian teak that we didn’t test would fare better. But the system is pricey ($519 for a 13-piece set), and the space you’re offered on the actual cutting surface is limited, so there’s not a ton of room for actual chopping—you dedicate a lot of the counter real estate to the attachable containers. If you’ve been in the market for nice prep containers just as much as you have been for a cutting board and love the idea of a smartly designed holistic system, you’ll like the Chef Station. We love the design in theory, but on the merits of the cutting board alone, it’s not a test winner.

Maple Wood Kitchen Basic Cutting Board.

The JK Adams Maple Wood Basic Cutting Board is made of durable maple. It has a minimal design with no embellishments and won’t add too much height to your prep zone. At just ¾" thick, it’s the thinnest wood board tested. The 17" x 14" footprint also offers a decent amount of space for cutting and chopping but is compact enough to keep in a small kitchen.

The JK Adams Pour Spout Cutting Board stands out because it has a juice groove and a pouring spout on both sides, making it truly reversible for cutting meat. Though this is a sizable board at 20" x 14", the groove and spout do take up a significant portion of the surface area available for cutting, so keep that in mind if you’re looking for something to use for really large cuts of meat. The wood is light-colored and will show stains from something like beets, but keeping it treated with beeswax and mineral oil will provide some stain resistance.

Material Kitchen’s MK Free Board is made entirely of plant-based materials ("100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers," according to Material’s website). That last part is crucial—especially if you're concerned about microplastics—because this board has none, hence the name. It's dishwasher-safe and has a loop that makes it easy to pull out of a cabinet or hang from a hook. Overall, it’s a totally fine cutting board you can feel very good about using, but without some plant-based bumpers on the bottom, it won’t get a top spot in our rankings. While the microplastic-free material is wonderful in theory, it feels a bit harder on your knives, and because it doesn't have silicone corners, it’s more prone to sliding around on a quartz countertop. And without anything to soften its landing, the thinner, harder material is also fairly loud.

Silicone Cutting Boards Mats, Set of 3.

If you’re looking for a nonporous alternative to plastic, rubber is our first pick. But both natural and synthetic rubber cutting boards are pricey, so you might want to consider a silicone cutting board. It’s key to note that these are mats, not actual boards. But even at ⅛" thick, the material provided a reasonable barrier between the knife and counter. Silicone is flexible so it’s easy to fold into a U-shape to transfer ingredients to a pot or scraps to the trash. These mats are also dishwasher-safe even though they’re very easy to hand-wash. And since the entire mat is silicone, it’s very nonslip. These also have built-in grooves around the entire perimeter and a hole in the corner for hanging and so far, they haven’t held on to any stains (even from steamed beets) or shown any knife marks (even when we tried to make some). That said, some users on Amazon have reported knife damage to their mats, which could be a result of the silicone degrading. Though silicone is durable and heat tolerant, repeated exposure to high heat or sudden temperature changes can weaken its structural integrity, and it can hold on to stains.

The All Aboard cutting board from colorful cookware brand Great Jones is like the original Material reBoard’s bigger, curvier cousin. At 16" x 12", it’s massive for a plastic board, and it has a nice loop/handle for hanging. It’s made of BPA-free recycled plastic, and the textured surface is nice to cut on. It doesn't have any sort of silicone grip to keep it in place on the counter when cutting, but it does have a juice groove.

In a recent development, these double-sided boards come in three sizes; one side has a juice groove and the other has an indentation along the top intended to hold Caraway’s tiny Dot & Dash containers. The boards are made from eco-friendly birch, which is lightweight compared to other woods but feels more like maple when cutting. These boards are also pretty thin, so I have concerns about warping, though limiting exposure to moisture can help with that. The board also comes oiled, though it did hold on to some strawberry and beet stains—as we’d expect any wood board to do.

Architec Original Gripper Cutting Board.

This 14" x 11" polypropylene (plastic) cutting board is fine but nothing special. It comes in a variety of fun colors, it has a handle hole you can use to hang it, and it’s dishwasher-safe. One side has small rubber feet (a.k.a. the “nonslip gripper” base), which does keep the board stationary but also makes it so you can only use one side for chopping.

Epicurean Kitchen Series Cutting Board.

Recent findings suggest that as much as we love Epicurean’s multipurpose cooking utensil, the brand’s cutting board is a no-go. There’s much to like; the nonporous wood composite is dishwasher-safe and won’t warp or splinter like wood. Plus, it looks so much nicer than plastic. But one reason it’s so durable is that it’s so hard, which made everyone who tried it worry about their knife blades. It was also very loud to use. The pricier nonslip version (which also has a juice groove) was slightly more pleasant to use, but still not recommended.

Recent findings suggest that at 14.9" x 19.6", this versatile bamboo carving board from Meater (the wireless thermometer brand) offers great surface area. One side is solid and free from embellishments, while the other features a sizable juice groove and pouring spout. But the light-colored wood stained fairly easily in testing and required intense scrubbing after we cut beets on it. And we no longer recommend bamboo cutting boards because the surface is extremely hard on knife edges.

Steelport Steelcore Cutting Board.

The Steelport Steelcore cutting board is a thin, sexy board from the maker of the also sexy Steelport knives. It’s a dual-sided board; one side is thin, perfectly smooth end-grain walnut, and the other is a durable recycled paper composite material. Embedded between the two is a steel core to prevent the board from warping. The surfaces are incredibly smooth, and the composite side has a juice groove, which maintains the modern look of the end-grain side. Unfortunately, the board we received had hairline cracks which, without the steel core, would have probably knocked three corners off of this board. For such a pricey piece of gear, it wasn’t well-packaged for cross-country transit. But the fact that the board stayed fully intact even with three cracked corners is a testament to the strength of the steel core.

Industry observers note that made In’s tableware, cookware, and kitchen tools have a lot of fans at BA, and I wanted to love Made In’s edge-grain Butcher Block. One side is a solid butcher block surface without any grooves or embellishments, while the other features a juice groove. At 17.75" x 11.75", it’s also a nice size for massive cuts of meat or to use as a charcuterie board. Unfortunately, even though it’s “steamed for durability” and appeared to come oiled out of the box, the surface really indicated marks from the chef’s knife we used in testing, and beet juice seeped into and stained the knife marks.

Recent findings suggest that the Totally Bamboo Kauai bamboo board is totally fine. It looks nice enough, it’s lightweight, and it doesn’t stain as easily as other wood cutting boards. But the surface is harder than comparable boards, and in testing, it slid around quite a bit on the counter. It’s also a little high-maintenance for bamboo; you’re supposed to treat it with a food-grade mineral oil every few days for a month, then re-oil “as needed.”.

In a recent development, the Angled Board from Material, which is generally available in FSC-certified walnut or carbon wood (the latter is actually stained white oak), would certainly make an attractive addition to a modern kitchen. But in testing we found that the smooth laminate coating indicates knife marks quite easily. It was also surprisingly slippery when we were cutting vegetables.

Farberware Nonslip Plastic Cutting Board.

According to recent reports, despite its name, the Farberware Nonslip Cutting Board didn’t stay put on the countertop during testing. On the other hand, though it’s not entirely stable, it is a nice size (14" x 10"), and the plastic construction makes it dishwasher-safe.

Nicole Home Flexible Plastic Cutting Board Mats.

Cutting boards (especially plastic ones) have one job, and that is to provide a protective layer between your knife and your counter. These flimsy “cutting board mats” didn’t, well, cut it in that department. They also slid around a lot when we were testing. If pressed, I’d say this type of cutting board (er, mat) could be handy to have around to put on top of a wood cutting board or butcher block countertop to help keep the wood clean and avoid cross-contamination when handling raw meat, but wouldn’t use this for chopping, slicing, or dicing directly on a stone countertop.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing you need to decide on when choosing a cutting board is which material you prefer. Here’s a rundown of what's good and bad about each.

PROS: Plastic cutting boards are useful as a supplement to a larger wooden board because they are lightweight and easy to carry around the kitchen. They are inexpensive, and they can go in the dishwasher. According to food director Chris Morocco, plastic is also a less absorbent material than wood (and about the same as rubber), which means they won’t harbor bacteria as easily. They’re a great choice for cutting raw meat.

CONS: Plastic boards are harder on your knives than wooden or rubber boards. They will also get dinged up after heavy use, which makes them prone to trapping bacteria. Plastic boards will need to be replaced more often than their wooden counterparts. Some research reveals that microplastics in food could be linked to plastic cutting board use, but the research on the long-term health effects of microplastics remains unclear. You do run the risk of your cutting surface moving around a bit unless you go with one that’s designed to stay put like our top pick here. Chris recommends laying a damp dish towel, paper towel, or nonslip rubber mat under your plastic board to keep it steady. Again, we recommend using your plastic cutting boards supplementally, for less rigorous chopping tasks than your wooden chopping blocks.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: If you’re the kind of home cook who is a dishwasher devotee, isn’t quite ready to invest in a cutting board, or wants to cut up raw chicken one day and mince garlic the next and needs a board that can be a totally clean slate each time, then plastic boards are the pick for you.

Recent findings suggest that PROS: In general, wood is soft enough to protect your chef’s knife but still hard enough for smooth cuts, making it perfect for prepping everything except raw meat, Chris claims. (Though you can do that, too, if you’re willing to give them a thorough soapy hand-washing afterward.) Another thing we love about wood boards is that they tend to “heal” themselves (i.e., they close up those knife marks after use), which prevents germ-harboring grooves from forming and keeps them in good shape for longer.

In a recent development, CONS: These boards require the most maintenance because wood is the most absorbent board material out there. They’re prone to retaining odors and stains, which means cleaning and caring for them is extra notable—and requires more work than plastic or rubber. Scroll to the end for more on how to perform that care. We'll also note that an exception to the “easy on knives” rule is teak, which is a dense hardwood containing silica, a substance known to dull blades. So make sure to check which wood your board is made of, especially because teak boards tend to be less expensive.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Wood boards are best for those who care about beautiful objects and are game to give their kitchenware the care and attention it deserves—you know, the people who are regularly sharpening their knives, maintaining the seasoning on their cast-iron pans, and deep-cleaning their Dutch ovens.

Recent findings suggest that end-grain wood vs. Edge-grain wood.

In a recent development, wood cutting boards come in two styles: edge-grain and end-grain. In edge-grain cutting boards, the wood grains are aligned horizontally. In end-grain boards, the wood fibers are aligned vertically. End-grain boards are easier on your knives, because the knife blade slips between the fibers of the board rather than sliding across them. End-grain boards also self-heal better than edge-grain boards, because the fibers can come back together. End-grain boards dry more quickly than edge-grain boards because the individual fibers are more exposed to air. This means they require more regular oiling. However, they are also far less likely to crack than edge-grain boards.

It has been revealed that in previous versions of this review, we recommended edge-grain cutting boards because they tend to be less expensive. However, in our most recent revision we found plenty of end-grain boards that were within $20 to $30 dollars of their edge-grain competitors. Because the research really shows that end-grain boards offer better longevity and are better for knife care, we’ve opted to recommend boards only in that style for our top picks this time around. Even if you invest in one that’s expensive (our favorite from Boardsmith), it will last you a very, very with proper care—the cost per use just makes sense.

Rubber cutting boards used to be found only in restaurant supply stores, but they have become more available on the market for regular home cooks in recent years—though they are still as expensive as wood boards.

Industry observers note that PROS: The rubber boards were some of our favorites in testing, because the material is so responsive. It’s lovely to slice on this springy surface. Rubber is soft, so it’s extremely easy on knives. The material is also non-porous, and therefore won’t absorb bacteria easily and is scratch resistant. They tend to have slightly textured surfaces, which is helpful for keeping them steady on the countertop. They’re super durable. While they aren’t usually dishwasher-safe, they don’t need any mineral oil applied (unlike wood cutting boards, which do); just wash them with mild detergent and leave them to air-dry.

CONS: The only real cons here are that rubber cutting boards don’t have the luxe look and feel you get from a wood board. They also tend to be heavier and pricier than plastic ones.

Industry observers note that there’s a reason these boards are so commonly found in sushi restaurants—the bouncy, softer surface supports a slicing motion rather than a rocking motion, making it optimal for ultra thin-bladed Japanese knives. If you like a heavier Western-style knife and use a rocking motion while chopping, this might not be the right board surface for you. Rubber boards are also quite heavy and difficult to maneuver around the kitchen, and they don’t look as nice as wooden boards.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Rubber cutting boards are great for people who like to use Japanese knives and want to invest in a piece of equipment that will last them for years to come, but doesn’t require a whole lot of upkeep.

Cutting board materials we don’t recommend.

How do you clean a plastic cutting board?

As mentioned above, plastic cutting boards are the most low-maintenance option, as you can simply pop (most of) them in the dishwasher. Though, if you’re cutting meat or fish, you need to scrape off any remnants under cold water before throwing it in. In restaurant kitchens, people often have a metal scraper that looks a bit like a palette knife for this; your stainless-steel bench scraper or plastic pastry scraper can also work. It prevents the proteins from cooking into the board’s nooks and crannies in hot water.

How do you clean a rubber cutting board?

Use that same cold water scraping technique if you have a rubber board, then follow with a hot, sudsy soap-up. Both rubber and plastic boards can be left to air-dry because they aren’t prone to warping.

How do you clean a wood cutting board?

In a recent development, wood cutting boards are a different story than any of the above materials. They’re high-maintenance–but also beautiful, long-lasting, and soft on your chef’s knife. Since you’re using your plastic or rubber board for raw meat (right?), a scrape-down followed by a warm, soapy hand-wash is usually enough for wood boards. Just don’t forget the underside. If you constantly get only one side of the board wet, you are unevenly hydrating the wood. Keep that same idea in mind when cutting: If your board is reversible, try to use both sides of it. If not, chop in different zones of your board to keep the surface evenly worn. That might sound like a lot, but if you chop in the same 2" quadrant daily, the angle on your board will promptly change, which can cause slippage and, eventually, dull knives. Drying is the last, crucial step. With a clean dish towel, dry your board as thoroughly as possible. Then prop it up on its side until bone-dry to further guard against warping or cracking.

Because knife-friendly wood can harbor bacteria and is prone to staining, an occasional sanitizing session is necessary—and if you are using your wood board for meat, those sessions should be more frequent. Sprinkle any stained areas with coarse salt and rub them with the cut side of half a lemon. To disinfect, dilute some white vinegar with water and spray the surface of your board. Let it sit for a couple minutes before washing and drying. If necessary, you can also sanitize your wood board with a bleach solution, but be sure to dry and then oil it really well after.

Sources indicate that POST-CLEANING CARE: Beyond washing, wood boards need to be treated with some TLC. Step right this way for an in-depth explainer on how to clean and care for it, but here’s the gist: At least once a month, pull out a clean microfiber cloth, a food-grade mineral oil, and a food-safe board sealant that combines oil with a protective beeswax. This is just as true if you have an inexpensive teak, acacia wood as it is if you go with something pricier, like a cherry or walnut cutting board.

Rub a small bit of the oil onto every surface of your dry, clean board. (You want the board to be really dry before you do this, so as to not seal in moisture.) Follow with the balm, which will buff into a creamy consistency. Don’t wipe that away just yet. Leave your board to deep-condition overnight, and then in the morning, gently wipe away any extra with a cloth or paper towel.

Breaking: You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint.
  • Frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option.
  • Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. And the most involved, time-consuming dish is undoubtedly the turkey. The centerpiece of your holiday table needs hours in the oven and at least a day of brining, but don't forget the time it takes to defrost beforehand, too.

Frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option. But they do require a little extra TLC and planning. So if you buy a frozen bird this year, you'll need to know how to work with it.

Making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely. Like chicken, turkey can spread Salmonella and other harmful bacteria. You should exercise caution at every stage of the process, including thawing, to avoid making your guests sick. Here’s what you should know.

Industry observers note that the USDA indicates it's also safe to defrost turkey in cold water, but in our opinion, it's not worth the hassle. The best bet is to thaw it in the refrigerator, where the bird can gradually defrost at the safe temperature with less risk of bacterial growth. What you should never do: thaw it on the counter, in the garage, or with warm water.

These environments are less controlled and can expose the turkey to the temperature danger zone (between 40°F and 140°F), where germs grow rapidly. Even if the center of the turkey is still frozen, the thawed exterior can become a hotbed for Salmonella by the time you're ready to roast.

Sources indicate that roasted turkey drippings make great gravy. But raw turkey juice dripping all over your fridge? Not so much. Even shrink-wrapped birds can leak, so you should always store your turkey on a baking sheet or roasting pan while it thaws.

Recent findings suggest that food safety experts also recommend storing raw meat on the lowest shelf. That way, any leaks are less likely to drip onto other ingredients in your fridge.

Industry observers note that we know you're probably keeping a lot of other ingredients in your fridge, so it can be hard to set aside extra room for the turkey. That said, it's a step worth doing. Giving your turkey plenty of personal space minimizes the risk of raw meat or its juices coming into contact with other ingredients.

In the event that your turkey does contaminate another ingredient, here's what to know: Foods that won’t be cooked, like salad greens, should be tossed if they’ve come into contact with raw turkey juices. Cooking contaminated foods thoroughly can kill harmful bacteria, but you’ll also need to clean any surfaces the juices touched.

In a recent development, turkeys are massive, so they take a long time to thaw all the way through. The experts at Butterball say you should allocate a day for every four pounds of turkey if you're keeping it in the fridge. That means if you're working with a 16-pound bird, set aside four days just for defrosting. Once it's fully thawed, Butterball claims your turkey will stay safe in the fridge for up to four days.

And on top of that, brining can make your turkey even more flavorful. If your frozen bird didn’t come pre-seasoned, consider setting aside another day or two for that step. (Want some guidance? Check out our brining guide.).

It’s extremely notable to keep things clean while you’re handling a turkey. One of the most common ways Salmonella spreads in the kitchen is through cross-contamination caused by poor hygiene.

So wash those hands (including under your fingernails!) with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Make sure you also thoroughly clean any utensils and surfaces that come into contact with raw turkey or its juices using hot, soapy water.

And above all, don’t stress! Americans prepare millions of turkeys every Thanksgiving, so you're not alone in your turkey-roasting journey. Follow the tips above to ensure yours turns out safe to eat and delicious.

Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The one thing that can make classic apple pie better?
  • According to recent reports, welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
  • 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so proposal ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

According to recent reports, welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Industry observers note that whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

In a recent development, make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Industry observers note that stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

In a recent development, place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Hating Turkey Doesn’t Make You Cool

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I admit to the light thrill it gives me to tell people that I hate oat milk, or that I prefer a wet martini.
  • Industry observers note that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop.
  • You would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is fun to be contrarian. I admit to the light thrill it gives me to tell people that I hate oat milk, or that I prefer a wet martini. It’s healthy for all of us to have our preferences. But sometimes what should be a matter of personal taste goes viral, amassing an army of haters who make this preference their entire personality. Think back to the great cake vs. pie wars of the 2010s, when anyone who admitted to liking cake was a tasteless rube. This isn’t even about what you like anymore—it’s about the attention that comes with going against the mainstream.

Industry observers note that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop. It is good, and I need people to stop pretending as if it’s not.

You would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother. In 2020, Business Insider wrote that turkey isn’t good and you should leave it off your Thanksgiving table. Vox insists the (horrifying) numbers of turkeys wasted every year are in service of “a dry, flavorless bird no one likes,” while Milk Street claims anyone who likes it must be “pretending.” Even this very publication called it “The Big Freaky Chicken.”.

In a recent development, respectfully, what on earth are you people talking about? Every year I cannot wait for the unveiling of the turkey. It is the ultimate reminder that this isn’t a normal meal because we do not eat turkey on the regular.

According to recent reports, over the years, my family has more often entrusted me with the cooking. We tend to do a version of this Martha Stewart en papillote method and I relish in the work. There is care required to ensure the meat is juicy and golden, and the resulting gravy silky and rich. There is great satisfaction in carrying out the gorgeous centerpiece. There is a subtle butteriness to the meat, and something wilder that even the most factory farmed bird can’t erase. Roasting a chicken is for a Tuesday. Roasting a turkey is for when you have the day off work.

Part of the joy of the turkey, of course, is the leftovers. Turkey congee, turkey pot pie, turkey melts, which will only exist because of Thanksgiving. A feast stretched out, reminding you that abundance does not last for just a day. Do not rob yourself of such plenty.

Obviously, the haters have not stopped millions of turkeys from being served every Thanksgiving. The biggest complaint seems to be that the turkey is never cooked well. And I’ll give you that, with a bigger bird, that you only encounter once a year, it takes planning and effort to ensure the middle doesn’t become a powdery mess while the legs are still raw. But I don’t know, try. There are many things that are tricky to cook that are beloved precisely because of the exhilaration of the challenge, so I don’t know why turkey gets all the heat.

In a recent development, if you’re here, it means you like to cook, even love it, and there are no shortage of recipes guiding you toward bird nirvana. So put your hobby to good use, get a meat thermometer, and figure it out. Because as much fun as it is to be a hater, it’s even more fun to prove everyone wrong with a feast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

According to recent reports, whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

In a recent development, turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Industry observers note that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

According to recent reports, unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

Sources indicate that the giveaway is pretty straightforward: Starting at 11 a.m., customers can visit select participating Panera locations and receive a free baguette with any in-café purchase. Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

According to recent reports, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first vital step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

It has been revealed that add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Sources indicate that nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

It has been revealed that let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

Industry observers note that cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

Mario Sorrenti: The Life Behind the Images

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that during Paris Photo, I visited Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, an exhibition curated by Aaron Stern at LSD, a small gallery on Rue de la Folie Méricourt, in a space that once housed a photographic laboratory.
  • I found myself wondering what drew them so strongly to these objects.
  • The more I looked at Mario's diaries, the more I felt that the answer lay somewhere in that last possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that during Paris Photo, I visited Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, an exhibition curated by Aaron Stern at LSD, a small gallery on Rue de la Folie Méricourt, in a space that once housed a photographic laboratory. The room was packed, almost overwhelmingly so, and what struck me immediately was the number of young people there. A generation that has grown up with smartphones, accustomed to producing and consuming images at an unprecedented speed, seemed completely fascinated by these handmade books, filled with photographs, Polaroids, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of a life lived more than thirty years ago.

I found myself wondering what drew them so strongly to these objects. Was it nostalgia for a time they had never experienced? A fascination with the physicality of photography, with the idea that images once existed as tangible things, objects to be touched, collected, cut, pasted and preserved? Or perhaps something more profound: a longing for authenticity, for the traces of real experiences, for a relationship with images that feels increasingly distant from the way we encounter them today?

The more I looked at Mario's diaries, the more I felt that the answer lay somewhere in that last possibility.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Industry observers note that mario Sorrenti is one of the defining photographers of his generation, an artist whose work has profoundly influenced the visual language of fashion photography since the early 1990s. His contribution to Vogue Italia alone is extraordinary. Over the years, he has created an extensive body of editorials that remain part of the magazine's visual history, images that helped shape not only the aesthetics of fashion but also the way fashion could communicate desire, intimacy and emotion.

Recent findings suggest that his signature is unmistakable, yet it cannot be reduced to a particular technique or aesthetic formula. There is the extraordinary sensitivity with which he approaches light, whether soft and natural or dramatic and carefully controlled. There is his attention to skin, texture and the physical presence of the body, his ability to move between the immediacy of a seemingly spontaneous photograph and the formal sophistication of an elaborately constructed image.

Above all, there is his particular way of representing sensuality.

Recent findings suggest that fashion photography has always had a complex relationship with desire, and Mario certainly wasn't the first photographer to explore intimacy or eroticism. But he brought something distinctly his own to that tradition. In his photographs, sensuality never feels imposed on the subject. It seems to emerge from the relationship between the photographer and the person in front of his camera. Even when an image is provocative, there is often a tenderness, a vulnerability, an emotional proximity that prevents it from becoming merely an exercise in seduction.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most famous example remains his photographs of Kate Moss, who was his girlfriend at the time, particularly the images that led to the iconic Calvin Klein Obsession campaign in 1993. Their extraordinary power came not simply from Kate's beauty or Mario's photographic talent, but from the genuine intimacy of their relationship. These were not images in which intimacy was staged for the camera. They emerged from an existing emotional connection, from a shared life, before becoming part of the collective visual memory of an era.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

And this is where the exhibition in Paris becomes especially revealing.Rather than presenting the celebrated photographs that established Mario's reputation, it turns its attention to the world from which those images emerged.

According to recent reports, the five diaries, spanning the years between 1991 and 2000, bring together photographs, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of everyday life. For the exhibition, Mario reproduced the pages of his original journals using color Xerox machines, then reassembled and bound them by hand. These are not conventional photographic books, nor simply archival documents. They occupy a fascinating territory between memory, artistic experimentation and the physical act of making.

There are portraits, faces, bodies, moments of everyday life, images of friends and lovers, familiar figures from the fashion world, and deeply personal traces of the people who surrounded him. There are handwritten words, repetitions, experiments, sequences of images that seem to follow the associative logic of memory rather than the conventions of photographic editing.

Recent findings suggest that what makes this particularly fascinating is that Mario's diaries were not simply something he created alongside his photographic career. They were fundamental to its development. He began taking pictures in Newly introduced York in the late 1980s, teaching himself photography while documenting the world around him, even building a darkroom in his mother's laundry room. It was precisely these personal diaries that, when he showed them to Calvin Klein in 1993, inspired the iconic Obsession campaign.

It has been revealed that the boundary between personal work and commissioned photography was never as clear as we might imagine. For many great photographers, this distinction becomes almost meaningless. It is precisely their personal vision, shaped by experiences, relationships and an ongoing process of exploration, that makes their work immediately recognizable, regardless of the context in which it is created. At its highest level, fashion photography is no longer simply in the service of a product, but becomes a space for genuine artistic exploration.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Recent findings suggest that the photographs are inseparable from the people Mario loved, the places he inhabited and the cultural atmosphere that shaped him. What emerges is not only the development of a photographic language but the formation of a sensibility.

I was particularly touched by this because I lived in Latest York during those same years. Mario and I belong to the same generation, and although our experiences were our own, we inhabited the same city, at the same moment, within a cultural world that was undergoing an extraordinary transformation.

New York in the 1990s was a place of intense creative exchange, where fashion, photography, music, art and nightlife constantly intersected. There was a sense of freedom, experimentation and possibility, but also a rawness, an urgency, a willingness to take risks and to blur the boundaries between one's personal life and creative work.

Sources indicate that looking through Mario's diaries, I recognized something of that world. Not necessarily the same people or the same experiences, but the atmosphere, the energy, the particular feeling of being young in a city where life and creativity seemed impossible to separate.

There is also the extraordinary family Mario comes from, a remarkable constellation of creative talent. His mother, Francesca Sorrenti, a woman of exceptional talent and an enormously influential figure in the worlds of fashion and image-making; his sister Vanina, an extraordinarily gifted photographer in her own right; and his younger brother Davide, who died tragically young in 1997, an exceptional photographer whose work captured the spirit of a generation with rare sensitivity and immediacy.

According to recent reports, in this family, photography has never been simply a profession. It has been a shared language, a way of relating to one another and to the world. Perhaps this helps explain why Mario's work feels so deeply personal, even when it is created within the highly sophisticated machinery of the fashion industry.

Sources indicate that davide's presence in the diaries is particularly poignant. Knowing his story, these images become more than fragments of a shared youth. They are traces of a relationship, of love, of loss, of a world that no longer exists except through the images that remain.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries, LSD Paris.

And this brings us back to something fundamental about photography: its extraordinary relationship with time.

It has been revealed that A photograph preserves a moment while simultaneously reminding us that the moment is gone. But in Mario's diaries, this relationship becomes even more complex. Photographs are placed alongside words, drawings, other photographs, fragments of thought. They are revisited, rearranged, reproduced and transformed. Memory becomes an active creative process rather than a passive act of preservation.

The use of Xerox is especially interesting in this respect. Reproduction here is not simply a means of copying an original. It becomes part of the artistic language itself. The texture, the imperfections, the altered colors, the materiality of the pages all contribute to the emotional experience of the work. The diaries remind us that photographs have a physical existence, and that the way we handle, sequence and preserve them can be as meaningful as the images themselves.

In an era when billions of photographs circulate through our screens, when images are increasingly detached from physical objects and, with artificial intelligence, can even be generated without any corresponding lived experience, this feels particularly significant.

We photograph everything, store everything, share everything. Yet how often do we return to those images and give them the attention necessary to become part of our memory? Mario's diaries speak instead of time spent looking, selecting, arranging, touching and remembering: the physical labor of creating meaning from the fragments of one's existence.

And perhaps this is why that small gallery in Paris was so crowded with young people.

In a recent development, I don't think their fascination was simply nostalgic. Nostalgia implies a desire to return to something we have lost, but many of those visitors had never known the world these diaries describe. Perhaps what they were responding to was something more immediate and universal: the evidence of a real life, with all its beauty, contradictions, intimacy and imperfections.

In a recent development, we often discuss the signature of a photographer in terms of light, composition, color or technique. But perhaps the most distinctive element of an artist's visual language lies somewhere deeper, in the particular way they have experienced the world. Before an image becomes iconic, before it enters the history of photography or the collective imagination, it begins with someone looking at something, or someone, and feeling compelled to remember.

Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000, curated by Aaron Stern, is on view at LSD, 20 Rue de la Folie Méricourt, Paris, from November 12 to December 10, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

In a recent development, reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

Industry News: Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

💡 Key Takeaways
