#77423. Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Upcoming York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1260 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Upcoming York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

According to recent reports, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a upcoming role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

Sources indicate that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

Sources indicate that as the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing newly introduced rituals to form.

The evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Newly introduced York.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

According to recent reports, the table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as rapidly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

According to recent reports, at the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

Sources indicate that for dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

According to recent reports, as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in Upcoming York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#77422. I Tested 6 Popular Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies to Find the Best One for Thanksgiving Dinner

I Tested 6 Popular Store-Bought Pumpkin Pies to Find the Best One for Thanksgiving Dinner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1159 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie.
  • Industry observers note that planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook.
  • Recent findings suggest that I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the massive day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

Industry observers note that planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook. There are many moving parts, and it can certainly be overwhelming when there is a houseful of hungry guests ready to dive into the biggest family meal of the year. That’s why I think there is no shame in turning to store-bought options for some elements of the meal. If baking isn’t your forte, but you still want to offer a traditional pumpkin pie for dessert, stores across the country are ready to help.

Recent findings suggest that I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the massive day. The contenders are:.

Sources indicate that I sampled and ranked each one based on overall appearance, the flavor and texture of the crust, and, finally, the consistency of the filling and spices used. I was certainly surprised by my top choice.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

The pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

In a recent development, this pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

Recent findings suggest that bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

In terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that at almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, the pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

Which store-bought pie is your fave? Let us know in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ciara has one request for whoever’s in charge of Christmas dinner: Please, whatever you do, make sure you’re up for the assignment. She’s willing to embrace a little holiday mess, but apparently, there’s a limit to how far that generosity extends into the kitchen.

“All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”.

Ciara, a mom of four, certainly understands how quickly the festivities can get away from you. “Christmas in our house is full of love, excitement and a little chaos,” she stated in a statement. But when it comes to the actual Christmas menu, she’s got some traditions she’s pretty attached to, many of which go all the way back to her childhood in Atlanta, Georgia.

In a recent development, "If you know one thing about us ATLians, you have Thanksgiving on Christmas. The same meal comes back around again," she told Delish.

And we’re talking a serious Southern spread: turkey legs, mac and cheese, candied yams, collard greens, chitlins, and pig feet. She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

#77418. Tech Report: A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

Tech Report: A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • Industry observers note that on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she remarked. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

Industry observers note that on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a big bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur noted. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

The Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

Sources indicate that venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

Industry observers note that chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in Latest York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

Recent findings suggest that “You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

If, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

According to recent reports, in 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

You’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

Industry observers note that hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

According to recent reports, be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

Industry observers note that on the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

According to recent reports, on Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

It has been revealed that at Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

In a recent development, among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

It has been revealed that the Colmado, Bur indicates, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

In a recent development, at the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, big sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

Sources indicate that one couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

At night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

Smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter said, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

#77415. BA's Best Lasagna

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

BA's Best Lasagna

📅 07 Feb 2018 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it.
  • The secret weapon is the meat sauce.
  • One step you can skip: boiling the noodles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this lasagna recipe has “rainy Sunday cooking project” written all over it. Layers of slow-cooked pork-and-beef ragù, silky Parmesan béchamel, and pasta bake into a rich, creamy lasagna Bolognese with a browned top and crisp edges. Make the sauces ahead to break up the work, or settle in for a day of very good kitchen smells.

The secret weapon is the meat sauce. Why make meatballs only to break them apart? Searing the meat in large balls leaves room for moisture to escape, so you get deep browning instead of a potful of steam. After a long, gentle braise, a potato masher turns them into ragù. Whole canned tomatoes, crushed by hand, give you control over the sauce’s chunky texture.

One step you can skip: boiling the noodles. In side-by-side retests, regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil!) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. The ragù and béchamel provide enough moisture to cook the pasta in the oven—as long as every noodle is covered. Spread the sauces to the edges, leaving no dry patches, and making sure the sauce totally covers the top layer of noodles before baking. Round it out with homemade garlic bread and a Caesar salad.

Do I need to buy no-boil lasagna noodles?

No—use regular dried lasagna noodles, preferably De Cecco. Skipping the boiling step isn’t the same as using noodles labeled “no-boil.” In our original tests, those absorbed too much sauce, leaving the finished lasagna drier than we wanted.

De Cecco Lasagne No.1 Pasta, 16-oz.

Why doesn’t this lasagna have ricotta or mozzarella?

This is a lasagna Bolognese, built around meat ragù and Parmesan-enriched béchamel rather than a separate cheese filling. The béchamel supplies the creaminess, while Parmesan brings salty, nutty flavor. For a less involved version with a cheese filling, try our Cottage Cheese Lasagna.

What’s the best way to split up the work?

Make the ragù one day, then tackle the béchamel, assembly, and baking the next. For an even lighter second day, make both sauces ahead and refrigerate them separately; rewarm the béchamel just enough to loosen it before layering. The ragù can be refrigerated for up to 4 days or frozen for up to 3 months, while the béchamel can be refrigerated for 1 day.

Watch Chris make BA’s Best Lasagna.

Save recipes and proposal every week with confidence. Download the app.

It has been revealed that saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

Industry observers note that preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Industry observers note that warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

In a recent development, using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

In a recent development, do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

According to recent reports, melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Recent findings suggest that note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

Recent findings suggest that if parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

Lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

In a recent development, do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

Recent findings suggest that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

It has been revealed that “Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

In a recent development, with which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Industry observers note that still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

According to recent reports, and Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Recent findings suggest that personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

Tech Report: Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
  • Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
  • Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

Alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and strategy on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

In a recent development, whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

Industry observers note that the first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have significant ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

Marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that showed me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from Latest England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

It has been revealed that there was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

It has been revealed that I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

Sources indicate that while my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was major sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Recent findings suggest that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Recent findings suggest that armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

According to recent reports, with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

Industry observers note that I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Sources indicate that there is a new vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

Recent findings suggest that with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Recent findings suggest that my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

In a recent development, we have a latest Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

Recent findings suggest that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

#77401. Tech Report: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1165 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Recent findings suggest that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Recent findings suggest that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Fresh York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

It has been revealed that while there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, stated that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

According to recent reports, part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Fresh York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she indicates. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

According to recent reports, but while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, states that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to latest takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she claims. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

The Best Recipes to Bring to a Potluck, According to Eater Editors

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

In a recent development, there’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a significant party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

It has been revealed that dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with significant flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

Industry observers note that I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.
